nodes.label: Spain/Argentina/Mexico ➤ Regional-Variant Marking Mechanism
nodes.rationale: Native-speaker consultants from Argentina, Mexico, and Spain supplied alternate regional terms marked with a ➤ arrow from the neutral/Spain headword, the book's stated selling point

nodes.label: Chapter 2 (Food) — Richest Three-Way Regional-Variant Chapter
nodes.rationale: Sustained three-way Spain/Argentina/Mexico contrastive food-vocabulary list (albaricoque/damasco/chabacano; aguacate/palta; etc.)

nodes.label: Chapter 6 (Housing) — Single Richest Regional-Variant Chapter
nodes.rationale: Densest three-way splits of any sampled chapter (frigorífico/heladera/refrigerador; grifo/canilla/llave), attributed to household appliances/domestic-space terms being independently coined per region rather than inherited from a shared Latin root

nodes.label: Chapter 8 (Car) — Flagship-Tier Regional-Variant Chapter
nodes.rationale: Automotive vocabulary fragmented across regions due to separate automobile-industry/import histories per country (maletero/baúl/cajuela; neumático/cubierta/llanta; parachoques/paragolpes/defensa)

nodes.label: Coger ➤ Tomar — Taboo-Avoidance Substitution (Travel Chapter)
nodes.rationale: coger (avión, tren) ➤ tomar in Argentina/Mexico; directly confirms the taboo-avoidance-naming pattern already flagged as a flagship finding in this corpus's Spanish Phase 1 work — coger is neutral in Peninsular Spanish but vulgar slang for intercourse across most of Latin America

nodes.label: Referential Gaps vs. Naming Variants (Products Absent in Argentina)
nodes.rationale: Explicit source footnote 'Productos y términos que no existen en Argentina' flags setas/chirimoya/chirla/cigala, and Spain's cava folds into generic champán in Argentina — a culture simply lacking a referent, not just naming it differently; relevant to conlang worldbuilding

nodes.label: Periphrasis vs. Lexicalization Across Dialects
nodes.rationale: Spain mints a dedicated verb/adjective (rebañar, granizar, climatizado) where American varieties instead use a descriptive multi-word phrase (pasar el pan por el plato, caer granizo, con clima artificial) — recurs across multiple chapters

nodes.label: Grammatical-Gender Dialect Variants (No Lexical Substitution)
nodes.rationale: Same root, different grammatical gender by dialect: pijama (masc. Spain/fem. Mexico), casete, secador/secadora and tostador/tostadora mirror-image gender-assignment mismatches — a pure gender-reassignment variant type distinct from lexical substitution

nodes.label: Diminutive-Suffix Regional Variants (-illa vs. -ita)
nodes.rationale: cucharilla/cucharita and mesilla/mesita — same root, different diminutive suffix choice rather than a different root entirely, a morphological rather than lexical variant

nodes.label: English-Loanword Regionalisms (Living, Shopping, Freezer, Jean, Airbag)
nodes.rationale: living (Arg., living room), shopping (Arg., mall), congelador/freezer (Arg.), pantalón vaquero/jean (Arg.), airbag/bolsa de aire (Spain loanword vs. Mexico calque), CD pronounced 'cidí' in Mexico
